analysis.one_liner: Makes community college tuition-free nationwide, with federal grants covering most costs, plus tuition aid at minority-serving colleges.
analysis.headline: The free community college bill died in a Senate committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have had the federal government pay 75% of average community college tuition and fees, with states picking up the rest, so students would pay nothing. States taking the money would have to make community college credits fully transferable to public four-year schools and align high school graduation with college readiness. It also would have paid minority-serving and historically Black colleges to waive or cut the first two years of tuition for low-income students, and set up a $1-billion-a-year fund for colleges to improve graduation and transfer rates. It died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Students attending public community colleges at least half-time would pay $0 in tuition and fees, with the federal government covering 75% of costs and states the remaining 25% (states could count existing need-based aid toward their share) [S3]. Low-income students at historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions would get up to 60 credits of tuition waived or sharply reduced [S2][S3]. States also would have to guarantee that community college associate degrees transfer fully to public four-year schools [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Community college students and low-income students at minority-serving colleges

how_it_helps.text: Waives community college tuition and fees entirely ($0 charged) for eligible students enrolled at least half-time, with the federal government paying 75% of average tuition costs and the state or tribe paying 25%.
Grants to historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions cover or sharply reduce the first 60 credits of tuition for low-income students.
Requires states to make community college associate degrees fully transferable as the first two years of a bachelor's degree at public four-year schools, so credits aren't wasted.
Provides a Student Success Fund ($1 billion per year) for colleges to add advising, childcare, transportation, and other supports shown to help students actually finish.

Includes automatic relief tiers so that when unemployment rises, the federal share rises — up to 95% — so states hit by recessions aren't forced to cut the program or raise other taxes to keep it going.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through open-ended appropriations ("such sums as may be necessary") for the tuition waivers and a $1 billion annual Student Success Fund [S3]. States would also have to maintain their higher-education spending and contribute 25% of costs, though relief tiers during high unemployment could lower the state share to as little as 5% [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, with states contributing a quarter of costs

drawbacks.text: The open-ended federal appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') means the true cost to federal taxpayers is uncapped and would likely reach tens of billions of dollars per year.

States must cover 25% of costs and maintain their own higher-education spending; the relief tiers that lower the state share kick in only during periods of elevated unemployment, and states that decline to participate get no benefit for their students.

Waiving tuition and fees does not cover living costs — housing, food, transportation, and childcare — which are often the larger barrier for low-income students, though the bill pushes colleges to help students access benefit programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and concrete: students would pay no tuition or fees at public community colleges, and low-income students at minority-serving institutions would get their first two years covered [S2][S3]. The main cost is fiscal — federal spending that could be tens of billions per year, since the community college program is funded at "such sums as may be necessary" [S3]. A serious design concern is the 25% state match with unemployment-triggered relief tiers: states could time relief requests to shift costs to Washington, and states that refuse to participate leave their residents without the benefit. Critics also note that "free tuition" addresses price but not other costs like housing and childcare, though the bill does allow states to count need-based aid toward their match and encourages colleges to help students access benefits [S3]. On balance, the bill would transfer substantial benefits to low- and middle-income families, paid for by general federal revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate's education committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 27, 2021 and read twice, then referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: no hearings, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and all bills not passed by then die.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a direct benefit from the bill's death, but opponents of federal spending on tuition-free college avoided a new open-ended entitlement, and states that would have had to put up matching money avoided that obligation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one directly; the program never started

for.name: 11 of 48 Senate Democrats (9 original co-sponsors plus 2 later cosponsors)
for.role: Senate cosponsors, including Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the 50 Republicans did.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — allowing it to expire at the end of the Congress.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support typically needed to advance in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 Senate supporters were Democrats or allied independents; none of the 50 Republicans cosponsored, and the committee controlled by the majority took no action.

industries.note: The bill would make community college tuition-free nationwide and direct federal money to these schools, while requiring them to improve advising, transfer pathways, and completion rates.

industries.industry: Public four-year colleges and minority-serving institutions (HBCUs, tribal colleges, HSIs)
industries.note: They gain grant money to waive or cut the first 60 credits for low-income students, but must adopt evidence-based reforms, meet performance goals, and cap tuition growth to participate.

The bill channels students and aid toward free public alternatives; for-profit schools, which compete with community colleges for the same students using federal aid, would face a cheaper (free) public competitor.
Students who no longer need to borrow for community college tuition would borrow less, shrinking the private lending market at the two-year level.
The bill authorizes open-ended appropriations for tuition waivers plus roughly $2.5 billion per year for minority-serving institutions by the early 2030s, financed by federal revenue.
